subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Above the anaerobic threshold, a performer is working:
options: Mainly aerobically with plenty of oxygen
questions.explain: Beyond the anaerobic threshold the body cannot supply enough oxygen, so it works anaerobically and lactic acid builds up.

questions.q: Which is an example of qualitative data?
options: A coach's description of a player's attitude
A player's sprint time in seconds
questions.explain: Qualitative data is descriptive and subjective, such as a coach's observations of attitude or technique.

questions.q: Which type of data would a Likert-scale questionnaire on how much a performer enjoys training mainly produce?
questions.explain: A questionnaire on opinions and feelings produces qualitative data about attitudes and enjoyment.

questions.q: Quantitative data is best described as:
options: Data based on opinions and feelings
Numerical data that can be measured
questions.explain: Quantitative data is objective and numerical, such as times, scores or heart rate.

questions.q: A performer scores 8, 10 and 12 on three throws. What is their mean score?
questions.explain: The mean is the total (30) divided by the number of throws (3), giving 10.

questions.q: The traditional Borg RPE scale runs from:
questions.explain: The original Borg scale runs from 6 to 20, where the value roughly relates to heart rate when multiplied by ten.

questions.q: Which type of chart is most suitable for showing how heart rate changes continuously over time?
questions.explain: A line graph best shows continuous change over time, such as heart rate during exercise.

questions.q: A performer records resting heart rates of 60, 62, 64 and 66 bpm. What is the mean?
questions.explain: The mean is the total (252) divided by the number of values (4), giving 63 bpm.

questions.q: A 30-year-old trains in the anaerobic zone at 85% of maximum heart rate. What is their target heart rate?
If a graph shows heart rate returning slowly to resting after exercise, this section represents:
questions.explain: After exercise the heart rate gradually falls back to resting during the recovery period.

questions.q: A performer records times of 12, 14, 14 and 16 seconds. What is the modal time?
questions.explain: The mode is the most frequently occurring value, and 14 seconds appears twice.

questions.q: A 20-year-old wants to train at 70% of their maximum heart rate. What is the target heart rate?
On a graph of heart rate during exercise, a sharp rise at the start most likely shows:
options: The anticipatory rise and onset of exercise
questions.explain: Heart rate rises sharply at the start of exercise (and even just before it) to meet the increased demand for oxygen.

questions.q: A bar chart is most appropriate for comparing:
options: Separate categories such as scores for different teams
questions.explain: Bar charts are best for comparing values across separate, discrete categories.

questions.q: How would you calculate a 40-year-old's estimated maximum heart rate?
questions.explain: Maximum heart rate is estimated as 220 - age, so 220 - 40 = 180 bpm.

questions.q: On the Borg RPE (rate of perceived exertion) scale, a higher number indicates:
questions.explain: On the Borg scale, higher numbers reflect greater perceived effort and more intense exercise.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of quantitative over qualitative data?
options: It is based on personal opinion
It is easy to compare and analyse objectively
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical and objective, making it easier to compare and analyse reliably.

questions.q: Why is it useful to collect data when analysing performance?
options: It replaces the need for skill
It gives objective evidence to identify strengths and weaknesses
questions.explain: Data provides objective evidence to identify strengths and weaknesses and to set targets.

questions.q: What is the maximum heart rate of a 15-year-old using the standard formula?
questions.explain: Maximum heart rate is estimated as 220 - age, so 220 - 15 = 205 bpm.

questions.q: A pie chart is most useful for showing:
options: Change in heart rate over time
Proportions of a whole, such as percentage of training time per method
questions.explain: Pie charts show how a whole is divided into proportions or percentages.

questions.q: The aerobic training zone is generally regarded as roughly what percentage of maximum heart rate?
questions.explain: The aerobic training zone lies at about 60-80% of maximum heart rate, where the body works mainly using oxygen.

questions.q: A 50-year-old's estimated maximum heart rate using the standard formula is:
questions.explain: Maximum heart rate is estimated as 220 - age, so 220 - 50 = 170 bpm.
